concepts.label: Reproduction and Its Two Modes
concepts.cardText: Reproduction is a biological process by which living beings produce new individuals of their own kind, and this is how life on the Earth continues to exist. Every organism has a definite life span: it is born, grows, matures, reproduces and eventually dies. Living beings reproduce in two main ways: asexually, where a single parent produces offspring that are almost exact copies of the parent, and sexually, where offspring inherit a mix of characteristics from the two individuals. This mixing may lead to small differences between parents and their young ones, and accumulated over many generations such differences help living beings adapt to changing environments.

concepts.label: Vegetative Propagation in Plants
concepts.cardText: Asexual reproduction is seen in many unicellular organisms such as bacteria, amoeba and yeast and in simple multicellular organisms such as hydra and sponge. It is also seen in many plants. Plants with fleshy underground stems, such as potato and ginger, sprout new plants without producing seeds; money plant stem and sugarcane stem cuttings grow into new plants; and Bryophyllum leaves sprout tiny plantlets. All these are examples of vegetative propagation, which means that new plants arise from the vegetative parts, the growing parts of a plant. The key point is that this type of reproduction involves only one parent and hence produces genetically identical individuals.

concepts.label: Cutting, Grafting, Layering and Tissue Culture
concepts.cardText: Asexual reproduction produces genetically identical individuals. This natural process has been adapted by scientists and horticulturists to develop several methods of vegetative propagation, such as cutting, grafting, layering and tissue culture, which are widely used to propagate plants efficiently and enable farmers to cultivate desirable crops on a large scale. In cutting, shoot cuttings are planted in soil mixed with compost after removing the leaves from the lower half. In grafting, a stem piece of one variety (Plant B) is fitted into a slit on a rooted plant (Plant A) and the wound is protected until it heals. In layering, the middle part of a flexible, thin twig, for example of lemon, is buried under the soil, and after 10 to 15 days roots develop; the twig is then cut from the parent plant. Propagation by tissue culture, which uses the shoot tip (apical meristem), has revolutionised farming practices like banana farming, providing mass-produced healthy plantlets that eliminate virus-infected plants and ensure high yields.

concepts.label: Pasteur and the Origin of Microorganisms
concepts.cardText: Microorganisms such as the fuzzy patches that grow on cooked food left on the counter in warm weather, or the black patches on damp walls, raise the question of where they come from. For long, people thought living things arose spontaneously from non-living matter. Experiments by Louis Pasteur proved that new life always comes from pre-existing life. He found the germ theory of disease, strengthened the cell theory that all cells arise from pre-existing cells, and led to practices like food and instrument sterilisation.

concepts.label: Spore Formation in Fungi
concepts.cardText: In Activity 11.3 mould grows on a moist slice of bread kept in a warm, dark moist chamber; the mould grew from spores already present in the air, which settled on the moist bread and began reproducing rapidly. Spores are formed in a sac-like structure or on a swollen vesicle on a long strip of fungal hyphae, and are produced in huge numbers, millions from one mould colony. Spores are lightweight, usually single-celled and float easily through air currents, waiting for moisture and nutrients to germinate quickly into a new individual. The chamber was kept warm (25 to 35 degrees Celsius) because mould spores need warmth and moisture; lower temperatures slow or stop their reproduction, which is why we refrigerate perishable food. Fungi grow very fast by spore formation and degrade organic wastes and pollutants, and many antibiotics such as penicillin and amoxicillin are derived from fungi.

concepts.label: Sexual Reproduction and Meiosis
concepts.cardText: Sexual reproduction involves two parents in the formation of a new individual, so both parents contribute to the genetic material of the offspring. If each generation received the full set of chromosomes from both parents, the chromosome number would double in every generation; this problem is solved by a special type of cell division known as meiosis. Each species has a fixed number of chromosomes in its cells; chromosomes are thread-like structures in the nucleus that carry genetic information. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, each pair consisting of one chromosome from each of two different individuals, a total of 46. Meiosis forms gametes: the chromosome number of the parent cell (diploid) is reduced to half (haploid) in the daughter cells, which are used only for reproduction. In animals male gametes are sperm and female gametes are eggs; in plants the pollen grain contains the male gametes and an ovule contains the female gametes. During meiosis the chromosomes of each pair separate so that each gamete receives only one from each pair, so every human gamete has 23 chromosomes.

concepts.label: Parts of a Flower
concepts.cardText: Flowering plants, also called angiosperms, are the most diverse group of plants on the Earth, and flowers serve as reproductive organs in angiosperms. concepts.label: Pollinators and Pollination Strategies
concepts.cardText: Pollination depends on external agents called pollinators, such as wind, water, insects like bees and butterflies, or birds. Pollination by wind is seen in plants like wheat, maize and rice, where pollen grains are light and small, produced in large numbers, and the stigma is long and feathery to trap them. In aquatic plants such as Vallisneria and Hydrilla, pollination occurs through water, with currents carrying the pollen from one flower to another. Many plants, including sunflower, hibiscus and marigold, are pollinated by insects such as bees and butterflies; their flowers are often brightly coloured, produce nectar and give off fragrance to attract pollinators, and the pollen grains are large, sticky or spiny so they can attach to the insect's body, while the stigma is also sticky. Some flowers, like those of the coral tree and hibiscus, are pollinated by birds such as the Indian white-eye and sunbirds.

concepts.label: Fertilisation, Seed and Fruit Formation
concepts.cardText: Once pollen reaches a compatible stigma, pollen grains produce pollen tubes that grow down through the style into the ovary. The male gamete moves through this tube and arrives at the ovule, where it fuses with the egg cell. This fusion of gametes is called fertilisation and it marks the beginning of a new life. The fertilised egg is called a zygote, which later develops into an embryo. Meanwhile the ovary surrounding the ovules enlarges and develops into a fruit, while the ovules develop into seeds inside it. Seed dispersal takes place by wind or water and animals, and when conditions such as water, air and temperature are favourable the seed germinates and grows into a new plant. Sexual reproduction not only produces new plants but also creates variation, helping plant species survive and adapt.

concepts.label: Variation in Reproductive Strategies of Animals
concepts.cardText: Animals show a wide variety of methods of sexual reproduction, but all face the basic challenge of ensuring that the male and female gametes meet and that the young ones survive long enough to grow and reproduce. Fish, amphibians and insects produce several hundred to several thousand eggs at a time with yolk, which contains nutritive substances to nourish the developing embryos. Since the mother's body cannot provide so much yolk for so many eggs, the yolk is just enough to produce a larva, which hatches from the egg and gets nutrition by eating organic wastes like rotten food and manures. This larva is an intermediate feeding stage; once enough nutrition is accumulated a transformation takes place and the adult body is formed, as in butterflies and frogs. In contrast, reptiles and birds lay eggs, and each egg contains enough yolk to nourish the developing embryo until it hatches into a young one. In mammals the zygote grows and develops inside the female body, and mammals typically feed their young with breast milk for some time after birth. Some young are ready to find their own food at birth, whereas others need an extended period of post-hatching or post-birth feeding and care, depending on how long the embryo develops inside an egg or inside the mother's body.

concepts.label: The Male Reproductive System
concepts.cardText: The male reproductive system has organs that produce male germ cells called sperm and help them transfer to the female body. Sperm are produced in two oval-shaped organs called testes, present in a pouch of skin called the scrotum. The scrotum keeps the testes slightly cooler than normal body temperature, which is necessary for sperm formation. The testes also produce a hormone, a chemical that regulates different functions, which controls sperm production and causes the physical changes seen in boys during puberty. From the testes sperm travel through a long tube called the vas deferens, which opens into the urethra, a common passage for the urine and the sperm. Glands like the seminal vesicles and the prostate add fluids to nourish the sperm and help them remain active and move. Each sperm has a head containing genetic material and a long tail that helps it swim towards the egg.

concepts.label: Gametogenesis: How Reproductive Cells Are Made
concepts.cardText: The formation of gametes is called gametogenesis and takes place in the testes and the ovaries. Gametes are formed by meiosis, in which the number of chromosomes is reduced to half: in humans, body cells have 46 chromosomes but sperm and eggs have only 23. In males, gametogenesis results in the production of numerous tiny motile sperm, whereas in females it results in the formation of a single large egg. In sexual reproduction male and female gametes differ greatly in size, number and structure, and this asymmetry is seen across most of the animals.

concepts.label: Ovulation, Fertilisation and Implantation
concepts.cardText: At birth a girl's ovaries already have millions of immature eggs. From puberty onwards, usually one mature egg is released every month from one of the ovaries, which is called ovulation. Before ovulation the uterus starts to prepare itself and its inner lining becomes thick. As ovulation happens the egg travels from the ovary to the oviduct. Sperm swim through the reproductive tract and may reach the egg in the oviduct; if a sperm encounters an egg and succeeds in fusing with it, a zygote is formed. The inner lining of the uterus becomes thicker and richer in blood vessels. The zygote undergoes a series of mitotic divisions while travelling to the uterus, and implants into the inner lining of the uterus to receive nourishment for development. This implantation marks the beginning of pregnancy. In-vitro fertilisation (IVF) is a medical technique in which an egg and a sperm are combined outside the female body, usually in a laboratory dish, and the resulting fertilised egg is then implanted in the uterus.

concepts.label: Menstruation and the Menstrual Cycle
concepts.cardText: If an egg is not fertilised it remains viable for about a day and then degenerates. The inner lining of the uterus, which had become thick and rich with blood vessels to nourish a developing zygote, is no longer needed and sheds. This lining, along with some blood, leaves the body through the vagina; the process is called menstruation or a period and usually lasts 3 to 7 days. The cycle of ovulation, preparation of the uterus and menstruation repeats typically every 21 to 35 days, often around 28 days, beginning at puberty between the ages of 10 to 14 in girls and continuing till menopause around age 50. Menstruation is a sign of a healthy reproductive system, not something to be ashamed of. Hygiene practices include using clean menstrual products, washing hands with soap and water before and after changing a pad, changing pads every 4 to 6 hours or more often if the flow is heavy, and disposing of used products properly by wrapping them and not flushing them down the toilet.

concepts.label: Pregnancy, Childbirth and the Mother's Health
concepts.cardText: Pregnancy in humans lasts about nine months and is divided into three stages called trimesters. In the first trimester the fertilised egg develops into an embryo during the first two months and major organs start forming; from about the ninth week the developing embryo is called a foetus. In the second trimester the foetus grows bigger and stronger and the mother can usually feel its movements. In the third trimester the baby grows rapidly and gets ready for life outside the womb. The uterus protects and nourishes the baby throughout. During childbirth strong contractions of the muscles of the uterus help push the foetus out through the birth canal. After birth breastfeeding is essential because a mother's milk provides complete nutrition and protects the infant from many diseases. During pregnancy a woman's health plays a vital role in the baby's growth and safety: she should eat a balanced diet rich in proteins, vitamins and minerals, attend regular medical check-ups, follow her doctor's advice on light exercise and rest, and avoid harmful habits such as smoking, alcohol, or taking any medicines without medical advice.

concepts.label: Sexual Maturity, Infections and Contraception
concepts.cardText: Adolescence brings sexual maturation, meaning our bodies are becoming capable of reproduction. It happens gradually, like the production of sperm in boys and menstrual cycles in girls, but emotional maturity takes longer; being emotionally mature means handling feelings, communicating clearly and making thoughtful decisions. Responsible choices help prevent unplanned pregnancies and sexually transmitted infections and support healthy relationships. Because sexual activity involves close physical contact, some infections can be transmitted from an infected person to an uninfected one; these are called Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and include gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts and HIV, which can eventually lead to AIDS. Some of these are not curable yet, and using condoms can prevent their transmission and also help prevent pregnancy. Contraceptive methods include barriers like condoms or vaginal covers, oral pills that alter hormones, and intra-uterine devices such as copper-T, and surgical methods block the vas deferens in males or the fallopian tubes in females. Prenatal sex determination is strictly prohibited by law in India because self-selective abortion driven by gender preference can lead to a marked imbalance in the societal sex-ratio.

checks.criterion: States that sexual maturity comes gradually but emotional maturity takes longer, and being emotionally mature means handling feelings, communicating clearly and making thoughtful decisions.

keyPoints.text: These are called Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs) and include gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts, and HIV (which can eventually lead to AIDS). Some of these are not curable yet. Using condoms can prevent their transmission and also help prevent pregnancy.
keyPoints.followUp: What are infections passed through sexual contact called, and name some of them?

checks.criterion: States that sexually transmitted infections include gonorrhoea, herpes, syphilis, genital warts and HIV, some are not curable, and using condoms can prevent their transmission and also help prevent pregnancy.

keyPoints.text: Some of them act as barriers, like condoms or vaginal covers, which stop sperm from reaching the egg. Some methods involve medicines (oral pills) that change the release of eggs by altering hormones, though these may have some side effects. Another method is the use of Intra-Uterine Devices (IUDs), such as copper-T that are placed in uterus to avoid pregnancy
keyPoints.followUp: Name barrier and medicine based methods that prevent unwanted pregnancy.

checks.criterion: Names contraceptive methods: barriers such as condoms or vaginal covers that stop sperm reaching the egg, oral pills that alter hormones and the release of eggs, and intra-uterine devices such as copper-T placed in the uterus.

keyPoints.text: Surgical methods are also used to stop unwanted pregnancies. These include blocking the vas deferens in males or the fallopian tubes in females, so that the sperm and the egg cannot meet.

checks.criterion: States that surgical methods include blocking the vas deferens in males or the fallopian tubes in females, so that sperm and egg cannot meet.

keyPoints.text: The practice of self-selective abortion is a significant concern, often driven by a preference for a specific gender. This practice can lead to a marked imbalance in the societal sex-ratio. So, prenatal sex determination is strictly prohibited by law in India.

checks.criterion: States that self-selective abortion driven by gender preference can imbalance the sex-ratio, so prenatal sex determination is strictly prohibited by law in India.

acceptedExamples: Pause: protective devices such as condoms can be used during sexual activity to reduce the spread of STIs
Pause: a couple using oral contraceptive pills but not condoms is still at risk of sexually transmitted infections because pills do not act as barriers

misconceptions.wrong: Oral contraceptive pills also protect against sexually transmitted infections.
misconceptions.fix: Condoms can prevent transmission of STIs and also help prevent pregnancy; oral pills only change the release of eggs by altering hormones.
